I would keep it simple and stay with the local main pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. In Quzhou County, that rotation matches the climate and the way rain falls here. Wheat uses the cool season, and maize catches the summer heat and rain. I would not spread myself across too many crops, because at my age and with a middle-school education, I would rather run one system cleanly than chase too many markets and make mistakes. Grain is easier for me to manage, easier to sell, and the machinery and field work are familiar.

At the start of this season, my wheat is already in the field from last autumn, so my first job would be to protect yield: one irrigation around jointing if moisture is short, another around booting or grain filling if needed, steady nitrogen, and disease and aphid control only when pressure shows up. I would keep the stand even and avoid wasting water. After wheat harvest in June, I would move fast into summer maize on the same land. I would use hybrid seed for stronger yield, sow quickly after harvest, keep basal fertilizer straightforward, and rely mostly on summer rainfall with one irrigation if the field turns dry at the critical stage. I would control weeds early and spray only as needed for armyworm, corn borer, or leaf disease. For tillage, I would use rotary tillage before wheat and no-tillage direct seeding for summer maize so I do not lose time after wheat harvest. My goal would be steady yield, lower risk, and not overspending on inputs.
